narration: Welcome to the module on Patient Preparation and Specimen Collection for Nurses, prepared by Bodhi Learning Labs.
Accurate diagnosis begins long before the laboratory report is generated. It starts at the bedside, with proper patient preparation and correct specimen collection.
A simple mistake - the wrong label, improper fasting, a delayed transport - leads to an inaccurate result and inappropriate treatment.
In this first section you will learn what pathology testing is, where errors actually occur, and how to take a blood sample that the laboratory can use.

narration: Laboratory testing is divided into three phases.
The pre-analytical phase includes patient preparation, correct specimen collection, proper labelling and timely transport to the laboratory.
The analytical phase is the processing and testing of the specimen in the laboratory.
The post-analytical phase is the reporting and interpretation of the results.

Errors can occur in any phase, but most occur during the pre-analytical phase - which makes the nurse's role the decisive one. A sample collected at the wrong time or by the wrong technique gives a misleading result, forces a repeat test, adds to the patient's discomfort, and delays the start of treatment.

narration: The order of draw is the sequence in which blood collection tubes are filled during a venipuncture, and following it matters because it prevents additive carrying over from one tube to the next and altering the result.

lines: First, to maintain sterility and avoid contamination.
narration: The first tube is the blood culture bottle. It is collected first to maintain sterility and avoid contamination, which matters most when infection is suspected.

lines: Sodium citrate. Coagulation - PT, INR, APTT. Fill to the exact marked level.
narration: Second is the citrate tube, with a blue cap. It contains sodium citrate and is used for coagulation tests such as PT, INR and APTT. This tube must be filled to the exact marked level or the result will be wrong.

lines: Plain, or clot activator and gel. Biochemistry, LFT, KFT, serology.
narration: Third is the serum tube, with a red or yellow cap. It may be plain or contain a clot activator and gel separator, and it is used for biochemistry, liver function tests, kidney function tests and serology.
Fourth is the heparin tube, with a green cap. It is used for electrolyte testing and some special chemistry tests.

lines: EDTA binds calcium to prevent clotting. CBC, haemoglobin, blood grouping.
narration: Fifth is the EDTA tube, with a purple or lavender cap, used for haematology tests such as complete blood count, haemoglobin and blood grouping. EDTA prevents clotting by binding calcium.

lines: Sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate. Glucose - it prevents glycolysis.
narration: And last is the fluoride tube, with a grey cap. It contains sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate, and is used mainly for blood glucose, because it prevents glycolysis.

slides.title: The vials and what they are for

reveal.text: Cap | Additive | Used for | After filling
reveal.cue_narration_line: Each vial contains a specific additive that preserves the sample for a particular kind of test.

reveal.text: Yellow | Clot activator and gel - serum separator | Biochemistry and microbiology | —
reveal.cue_narration_line: The yellow top is a serum separator tube containing clot activator and gel, used for most biochemistry tests and for some microbiology and serology.

reveal.text: Red | None | Biochemistry and serology | Do not shake - allow to clot
reveal.cue_narration_line: The red top is a plain tube with no preservative, used for biochemistry and serology. It should not be shaken - the blood is allowed to clot naturally.

reveal.text: Purple | EDTA | Haematology - CBC, haemoglobin, peripheral smear | Invert gently several times
reveal.cue_narration_line: The purple or lavender top contains EDTA, an anticoagulant, and is used for haematology tests such as complete blood count, haemoglobin and peripheral smear. Invert it gently several times after collection.

reveal.text: Grey | Sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate | Glucose | Mix gently
reveal.cue_narration_line: The grey top contains sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate and is used mainly for glucose, because the fluoride prevents blood cells breaking the glucose down. Mix it gently.

reveal.text: Blue | Sodium citrate | Coagulation - PT, INR, APTT | Fill to the mark, then invert gently
reveal.cue_narration_line: The blue top contains sodium citrate and is used for coagulation studies such as PT, INR and APTT. It must be filled to the correct level and inverted gently.

reveal.text: Green | Heparin | Ammonia and special chemistry | Invert gently
reveal.cue_narration_line: The green top contains heparin and is used for ammonia and certain special chemistry tests.

reveal.text: Black | Sodium citrate | ESR by the Westergren method | Invert gently
reveal.cue_narration_line: And the black top contains sodium citrate and is used specifically for erythrocyte sedimentation rate, by the Westergren method.

reveal.text: Test | What is different | Why
reveal.cue_narration_line: Some tests need handling that nothing else does.

reveal.text: Blood culture | Collect before antibiotics. Strict aseptic technique. Two separate sites. | Antibiotics suppress growth; two sites improve detection
reveal.cue_narration_line: Blood cultures should always be collected before antibiotics are started, using strict aseptic technique and preferably from two separate sites, which improves the detection of infection.

reveal.text: ABG | Transport on ice if delayed | Cooling slows cell metabolism and preserves the values
reveal.cue_narration_line: Arterial blood gas samples should be transported on ice if there is any delay in processing.

reveal.text: Ammonia | Send immediately on ice | The level rises quickly if the sample is not handled properly
reveal.cue_narration_line: Ammonia samples must go to the laboratory immediately, on ice, because the level rises quickly if the sample is mishandled.

reveal.text: Lactate | Avoid prolonged tourniquet use | A prolonged tourniquet falsely raises the lactate
reveal.cue_narration_line: Lactate samples should be collected without prolonged tourniquet application, which falsely raises the lactate.

reveal.text: Troponin | Follow the serial timing | A single value cannot show the rise and fall of cardiac injury
reveal.cue_narration_line: And troponin is usually performed as a series at specific intervals, because the pattern over time is what identifies heart muscle injury.

narration: Welcome to Section 3, the final section of the module on Patient Preparation and Specimen Collection.
A correctly taken specimen can still produce a wrong result if it reaches the laboratory late, unlabelled, or in the wrong container.

In this section you will learn the transport requirements, what to document, the complications to watch for, what to teach the patient, how to segregate the waste, and the errors that most often spoil a sample.

narration: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
State the transport requirement for each specimen type.
Identify the critical specimens that need immediate transport.
Document a specimen collection completely.
Recognise the complications of blood collection, lumbar puncture and urine collection.
Segregate biomedical waste correctly.
And avoid the common errors that cause a specimen to be rejected.

reveal.text: Specimen | Transport requirement | Why
reveal.cue_narration_line: Proper transport preserves the sample. Delays or the wrong storage conditions cause bacterial overgrowth, cell destruction or chemical change, any of which alters the result.

reveal.text: Blood culture | Immediate | Delay reduces recovery of the organism
reveal.cue_narration_line: Blood cultures go to the laboratory immediately, because delay reduces the recovery of pathogens.

reveal.text: CSF | Immediate - do not refrigerate | Some organisms do not survive cooling
reveal.cue_narration_line: Cerebrospinal fluid also goes immediately, and must not be refrigerated. CSF is a critical specimen, especially where meningitis is suspected, and some organisms do not survive cooling.

reveal.text: Urine C/S | Within 1 hour | Bacteria multiply in the container and distort the count
reveal.cue_narration_line: Urine for culture should reach the laboratory within one hour. Beyond that, bacteria multiply in the container and the count is no longer meaningful.

reveal.text: Sputum | Early morning, then promptly | Overnight secretions give a more concentrated sample
reveal.cue_narration_line: Sputum is best collected early in the morning, when secretions have accumulated overnight, and sent as soon as possible after collection.

reveal.text: Stool for OBT | Avoid contamination | Urine, water or menstrual blood will alter the result
reveal.cue_narration_line: Stool for occult blood must be collected without contamination by urine, water or menstrual blood, any of which affects the result.

reveal.text: ABG | On ice if delay is expected | Cooling slows cell metabolism and preserves the values
reveal.cue_narration_line: And arterial blood gas samples are transported on ice if immediate analysis is not possible, because cooling slows cellular metabolism and preserves the oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH values.

narration: Accurate documentation gives traceability and protects the patient.
Record the date and exact time of collection, because some results depend entirely on when the sample was taken.
Record the type of specimen collected.
Record the name or signature of the person who collected it, for accountability.
Record any special patient preparation - fasting, a medication withheld, collection before antibiotics - because these influence the result.
And record any unusual observation: difficulty collecting the sample, haemolysis, insufficient quantity, contamination, or an adverse reaction such as dizziness or bleeding.
Enter all of it in the laboratory register, the nursing notes and the patient's medical record.

reveal.text: Procedure | Complications | What reduces them
reveal.cue_narration_line: Specimen collection is generally safe, but complications occur.

reveal.text: Blood collection | Haematoma, bleeding, syncope, infection | Correct technique and firm post-procedure pressure
reveal.cue_narration_line: During blood collection, the common ones are haematoma from blood leaking into the surrounding tissue, prolonged bleeding, fainting, and rarely infection at the puncture site. Proper technique and firm pressure afterwards prevent most of them.

reveal.text: Lumbar puncture | Headache, CSF leak, back pain | Lying flat as protocol specifies, and close monitoring
reveal.cue_narration_line: After a lumbar puncture, the patient may have a post-lumbar-puncture headache, leakage of cerebrospinal fluid from the site, or localised back pain. Close monitoring and correct positioning reduce these.

reveal.text: Urine collection | Contamination - bacteria, vaginal secretions, stool, water | Clean catch technique and a sterile container
reveal.cue_narration_line: In urine collection, the common problem is contamination - with bacteria, vaginal secretions, stool or water - which produces an inaccurate result and a repeat test.

narration: Specimen collection is generally safe, but complications occur.

reveal.text: Fasting instructions

reveal.text: Medication restrictions

reveal.text: The correct collection method — Midstream urine, deep sputum, stool technique

reveal.text: Why timely submission matters
reveal.cue_narration_line: And explain why the specimen must reach the laboratory promptly, because delay affects the quality of the sample and the accuracy of the result.

reveal.text: Avoid touching sterile areas
reveal.cue_narration_line: Maintain aseptic technique and avoid touching the sterile areas of equipment or containers, which would contaminate the specimen.

reveal.text: Use leak-proof containers
reveal.cue_narration_line: Use clean, intact, leak-proof containers, so nothing spills during transport.

reveal.text: Double-check labels

narration: Correct biomedical waste segregation protects healthcare workers and the environment.
Infectious waste, such as contaminated dressings and swabs, goes in the yellow bag.
Contaminated plastic items - tubing, gloves and syringes without needles - go in the red bag.
Sharps, including needles and blades, go in a puncture-proof white container.
And broken glassware and medicine vials go in the blue container.
Correct segregation is a nursing responsibility and a key part of infection control.

reveal.text: Drawing above an IV infusion line — IV fluid dilutes the sample
reveal.cue_narration_line: Do not draw blood from a vein above an intravenous infusion line, because the fluid dilutes the sample.

reveal.text: Underfilling the citrate tube — Coagulation results come out wrong
reveal.cue_narration_line: Fill the citrate tube to the marked level - underfilling produces an incorrect coagulation result.

reveal.text: Sending saliva instead of sputum
reveal.cue_narration_line: For sputum, make sure the patient provides deep respiratory secretions rather than saliva.

reveal.text: Non-sterile container for a culture
reveal.cue_narration_line: Always use a sterile container for a culture specimen.

reveal.text: Delay in transport
reveal.cue_narration_line: Avoid delays in transport, which alter the composition of the sample.

reveal.text: Incorrect fasting instructions
reveal.cue_narration_line: And give correct fasting instructions, because the wrong ones produce a result that cannot be interpreted.

narration: Let us summarise the key points of the whole module.
Pathology investigations are essential for accurate diagnosis, treatment planning and monitoring.
Most laboratory errors happen before the sample ever reaches the bench - in the preparation, the collection, the labelling and the transport.
Reliable results depend on correct patient identification with two identifiers, the right container, the correct order of draw and the correct fill level.
Follow the test-specific rules: fasting, timing, aseptic technique and any drug holds.
Blood cultures and cerebrospinal fluid go to the laboratory immediately, and CSF is never refrigerated.
Document the time, the specimen, the collector, the preparation and anything unusual, in the register, the notes and the file.
And teach the patient, segregate the waste correctly, and check the label twice.
Through careful preparation, correct collection and prompt transport, nurses make the laboratory result something a clinician can safely act on.
